ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: In the circuit shown in the figure, \(V_A = 3\text{V}\) and \(V_B = 0\text{V}\). If the forward voltage drop of the diodes is ignored, what is \(V_F\)?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure there are two input terminals VA and VB, each connected through a diode to the common node on the right; the directions of both diodes are from the left-side input toward the right-side common node. The common node is labeled VF, and this node is also connected downward through resistor R to -12 V. Therefore this is a diode OR circuit composed of two diodes and a pull-down resistor. Then reason: The problem gives VA = 3 V, VB = 0 V, and ignores the diode forward voltage drop, that is, the voltage drop when an ideal diode conducts is 0. The pull-down resistor will pull VF down toward -12 V, but as long as some input voltage is higher than VF, the corresponding diode will conduct and clamp VF to that input voltage. The higher of the two inputs is VA = 3 V, so the diode corresponding to VA conducts, making VF = 3 V; at this time, the diode with VB = 0 V is reverse-biased and cut off because its input terminal is lower than the output terminal. So VF = max(3 V, 0 V) = 3 V.

method.method_draft: First identify from the image that the circuit is a diode OR: VA and VB each connect through a diode to the common output VF, and R pulls VF downward to -12 V. From the text take VA = 3 V, VB = 0 V, and ideal zero forward drop. Apply the ideal diode-OR rule: the output follows the larger input because the higher input diode conducts and the lower input diode is reverse-biased. Therefore VF = max(3 V, 0 V) = 3 V.
